analysis.one_liner: Exempts mid-size banks from Dodd-Frank's strictest oversight unless the Fed finds they threaten stability.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 288-130 on December 19, 2017, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Dodd-Frank law, any bank holding company with $50 billion or more in assets automatically faces extra oversight from the Federal Reserve: tougher stress tests, plans for winding down safely, and stricter capital and risk rules. This bill scraps the automatic trigger. Only banks formally identified as "global systemically important" would face the strictest rules automatically; everyone else would be exempt unless the Federal Reserve makes a case-by-case finding that the bank threatens U.S. financial stability, and any category-wide designation would need a two-thirds vote of the Financial Stability Oversight Council. It also temporarily keeps collecting existing oversight fees from the newly exempt banks, capped at $58 million, to avoid an immediate funding gap.
analysis.who_benefits: Bank holding companies that hold $50 billion or more in assets but are not on the global systemically important list — typically large regional banks. They would escape enhanced supervision, stress testing, living wills, and stricter prudential standards unless the Federal Reserve affirmatively designates them. The bill gives the Fed 18 months after enactment to phase in the change.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the automatic $50 billion asset trigger with designation only for banks identified as global systemically important or found by the Federal Reserve to threaten financial stability, removing the strictest Dodd-Frank requirements from other large banks.

Lets the Federal Reserve subject non-designated banks to tailored supervision only through findings based on size, interconnectedness, substitutability, global activity, and complexity, and requires a two-thirds vote of the Financial Stability Oversight Council, including the Chair, to approve metrics for any category-wide designation.

Temporarily extends existing oversight fees to banks that lose their designation, capped at $58 million in total collections, so oversight funding does not drop immediately; affected banks can spread payments over up to 48 months.

analysis.who_pays: The financial system and, potentially, taxpayers. The banks that lose automatic oversight would no longer face the same stress tests, wind-down planning, and early-remediation requirements, so risk could build at large regional institutions without the same early-warning checks; a failure at one of them could still ripple through the economy. Oversight funding also shrinks after the temporary fee extension runs out.
analysis.who_pays_short: Financial system and potential taxpayer backstops

drawbacks.text: Banks that are large but not on the global systemically important list could build up risk without automatic stress tests, wind-down plans, or stricter capital rules; oversight would depend on the Federal Reserve proactively making a case-by-case or category finding, and any category-wide designation faces a two-thirds vote hurdle at the Financial Stability Oversight Council.

The bill tells the Federal Reserve to make designations only 'within the limits of its existing resources' and to use already-reported data to avoid burdening banks, which could constrain how aggressively the Fed examines companies that fall outside the automatic trigger.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the trade-off supporters themselves built into the bill: because removing designations cuts fee collections for oversight, the bill has to temporarily extend assessments on the newly exempt banks, capped at $58 million, recognizing that the oversight system loses its funding base under the new threshold.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill lowers compliance costs for a defined set of large banks, and its backers argue a fixed asset number is a crude way to judge risk. The cost is a weaker early-warning system: automatic oversight of every $50 billion-plus institution is replaced by a slower, discretionary process with a high vote threshold for category designations, and the bill itself concedes the funding gap by temporarily extending fees. The savings go to the banks; the added systemic risk is shared by everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 288-130 in December 2017, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 19, 2017, and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.

The committee marked it up in October 2017 and reported it amended on a 47-12 vote, and the House passed it on December 19, 2017, 288-130, with 229 of 238 Republicans voting yes and 59 of 193 Democrats.

The Senate received the bill on December 20, 2017, and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action was recorded before the Congress ended January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large regional banks won House approval of lighter oversight, but because the Senate never acted, the existing Dodd-Frank designations stayed in place for the rest of that Congress, and the oversight system's funding and authority were untouched by this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large regional banks, but only partially

for.name: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace the automatic $50 billion oversight trigger with case-by-case Federal Reserve designations.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Held hearings and markups, then reported the bill amended on a 47-12 vote on October 12, 2017.

against.name: 128 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 128 of 193.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 20, 2017, referred it to the committee, and never reported it or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Republicans were nearly unanimous in favor (229 of 238 voting yes), while Democrats split against it 128-59, and the bill died in a Republican-controlled Senate committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Large regional banks (roughly $50 billion-plus in assets, not globally systemically important)
industries.note: These banks would escape automatic enhanced supervision, stress tests, and stricter prudential standards unless the Federal Reserve affirmatively designates them, cutting their compliance costs. Their savings come at the cost of weaker checks on institutions whose failure could still threaten the financial system.

They keep their designation and the strictest rules under the bill. Relative to newly exempt regional banks, though, they gain a competitive edge, since their smaller rivals no longer bear the same oversight burden.
